Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Psychiatrist
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Avoid Sex: Sex, Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Dr. Leilani Ahina had always been a composed and confident presence in her work as a psychiatrist, but that all changed one fateful night two years ago when she was involved in a near-fatal car accident on the highway. She remembered driving home from a late-night shift at the hospital, feeling tired but alert, when suddenly a car swerved into her lane and crashed into her vehicle. The impact was immense, and Leilani's world went dark. When she came to, she was disoriented and in pain, but as the days passed, the physical wounds healed, and the memories of that night began to resurface. They were fragmented and disjointed, like a puzzle with missing pieces. She couldn't quite put the sequence of events together – the crash, the sirens, the hospital stay – it all felt jumbled in her mind. Even now, she couldn't tell a clear story of what happened, not even to herself. As the weeks went by, Leilani started noticing that certain things would trigger these memories without warning. She'd be driving to work and see a car with a similar make and model involved in an accident on the side of the road, and suddenly she'd be back in her own wrecked vehicle, reliving the terror. Or she'd hear the sound of screeching tires or shattering glass, and it would all come flooding back. She tried to avoid these triggers as much as possible – taking different routes to work, avoiding the news – but it seemed like they were everywhere. Leilani's colleagues noticed a change in her too. She became more withdrawn and hesitant, often questioning her own judgment and second-guessing herself. She'd always been confident in her ability to make sound decisions, but now she was plagued by self-doubt. What if she missed something? What if she made the wrong call? It was as if she'd lost faith in her own abilities. She also started to experience strange physical sensations – feeling jumpy and easily startled, always on edge. She'd wake up multiple times during the night, convinced that someone was lurking outside her bedroom window or that a fire had broken out in the house. She'd lie there for hours, listening intently, waiting for some sign of danger. As a result, Leilani started to avoid certain situations and activities altogether. She stopped seeing patients who reminded her of the accident – those with similar injuries or trauma histories. She avoided sex with her partner, feeling like she was somehow damaged goods. And she barely slept, too afraid of what might happen in the dark. Her own therapy practice suffered as well. Patients began to notice her distraction and lack of focus. She'd catch herself zoning out during sessions, lost in thought as memories of the accident crept into her mind. Her colleagues started to worry about her, suggesting she take some time off or seek help, but Leilani was too proud – she didn't want to admit that she needed it. One day, while working with a patient who had experienced a similar trauma, Leilani realized just how far she'd fallen. She saw the fear and doubt in this patient's eyes and knew she was staring at her own reflection. It was then that she finally acknowledged the toll the accident had taken on her life – the permanent damage it had inflicted on her sense of self and her worldview. Now, as she sits in her office, staring out the window at the city below, Leilani feels a mix of emotions: fear, shame, but also a glimmer of hope. She knows she needs help to process this trauma and regain control over her life. For the first time in two years, she's willing to confront the memories head-on, rather than trying to avoid them. With a newfound sense of determination, Leilani Ahina has decided to seek the very therapy she's been reluctant to receive – hoping that by facing her fears, she can learn to heal and find peace once more.
